title: On Reliable Numerical Evaluation of Extreme Gaussian Tail Probabilities
content: Extreme Gaussian tail probabilities arise in a wide range of statistical applications, including large--scale hypothesis testing, meta--analysis, and risk assessment. Although the normal distribution is analytically well understood, reliable numerical evaluation of the tail probability \[ 1-\Phi(Z) \] becomes challenging for large values of Z, due to the combined effects of numerical underflow, truncation of the infinite integration domain, and discretization error in numerical integration. In this work, we present a theoretically grounded framework for evaluating extreme Gaussian tail probabilities under standard double–precision arithmetic. Rather than introducing a new closed–form approximation, we reformulate the problem explicitly as a controlled numerical integration task and decompose the total numerical error into three independent components: underflow, truncation error, and numerical integration error. Central to this formulation are explicit analytical lower and upper bounds, F(Z) and G(Z), which satisfy \[ F(Z) \le 1-\Phi(Z) \le G(Z) \] and provide a rigorous enclosure of the true tail probability. Within this framework, numerical underflow is avoided by scale separation and logarithmic representations, truncation error is controlled by selecting a finite integration range based on the analytical bounds, and numerical integration error is regulated through standard quadrature error estimates. Numerical experiments show that, as $Z$ increases, the effective integration range shrinks and the required subdivision number remains moderate, explaining the empirical robustness of Gaussian tail evaluations observed in practice. The proposed formulation does not aim to compete with existing highly optimized implementations based on minimax rational approximations. Instead, it provides a transparent theoretical interpretation of why such implementations remain stable and accurate even in extreme regimes. By explicitly connecting classical analytical bounds with numerical error control, this work offers a principled perspective on Gaussian tail evaluation and clarifies the structure underlying long--standing numerical practices.
